source: Irving, Szegedy, Alemi, Een, Chollet, Urban (2016) DeepMath - Deep Sequence Models for Premise Selection
finding: First large-scale deep learning for premise selection on Mizar. Task: rank library facts for a conjecture so an ATP (E prover) can prove it. Perfect premise choice would raise ATP success well above what real selectors reach.
numbers: Mizar: 57,917 theorems, 32,524 (56.2%) ATP-provable with perfect premises vs 40% reached by an earlier 14-method portfolio (best single method 27.3%). Test set 2,742 theorems.
quote: with perfect premise selection (a perfect choice of library facts) ATPs can prove at least 56%
limits: Labels come from ATP-found proofs, so they are one of many valid premise sets. Prover is E with fixed time limit.
agent_relevance: Upper bound for retrieval: good fact choice is worth about 16 points over the best real selector then. Our subgoal library retrieval has the same headroom logic.

source: Irving et al. (2016) DeepMath, Table 1 and negative mining
finding: Neural rankers (char-CNN, word-CNN, def-CNN) roughly matched k-NN with hand features. Combining char and def models helped. Hard-negative mining was crucial.
numbers: With top-16 cutoff, negative mining raised proved theorems from 61.3% to 66.4% for the best neural model. At k=32: k-NN 39.4%, def+char-CNN 44.4%. Largest cutoff: k-NN 65.1%, def-CNN 66.4%, def+char-CNN 67.9%. Union def-CNN + k-NN 74.25%; union of all methods 80.9% (2218/2742); neural-only union 78.4%.
limits: Single neural model gain over k-NN is small; the big gain is from complementarity.
agent_relevance: Ensembles of different selectors beat any one selector. For an agent: retrieve from several indexes (statement, structure, usage) and merge.

source: Alama, Heskes, Kuhlwein, Tsivtsivadze, Urban (2012) Premise Selection for Mathematics by Corpus Analysis and Kernel Methods
finding: Pre-neural baseline: learn premise selection from minimal proof dependencies in Mizar with kernel methods. Learned selection beat the hand-crafted SInE filter.
numbers: Benchmark of 2078 large-theory problems; combined effect = 50% improvement over Vampire/SInE.
limits: Mizar only; features are symbols and terms; no semantics. I read the abstract and intro only.
agent_relevance: Learned relevance from past proofs beats syntactic heuristics. A subgoal library can log which entries solved which goals and learn from that.

source: Piotrowski & Urban (2020) Stateful Premise Selection by Recurrent Neural Networks
finding: Choose premises one at a time with an RNN that keeps a state, so later choices depend on earlier ones. Compared to XGBoost independent ranking.
numbers: E prover 10 s limit; baseline with all premises proves 9% of test theorems. Best NMT ATP score 0.40 vs XGBoost 0.31 (29% worse). Adding subproof training data gave +11 points over basic. XGBoost looked better on similarity metrics but worse on real ATP success.
limits: Similarity-to-human-proof metrics did not predict ATP success.
agent_relevance: Pick the next fact given what is already picked (set-aware selection), and judge by downstream solve rate, not match to a reference.

source: Wang, Tian, Wang, Cheng, Wei, Zhai (2017) Premise Selection for Theorem Proving by Deep Graph Embedding
finding: Graph embedding of formulas (FormulaNet) for premise ranking on HolStep.
numbers: HolStep accuracy 83% to 90.3% (conditional) and 90.0% (unconditional). With zero graph update steps it still gets 81.5%, so most signal is in constant names alone. Diminishing returns after 3 steps.
limits: HolStep is binary classification of useful statements, not proof success.
agent_relevance: Symbol names carry most signal; structure adds about 9 points. Cheap lexical overlap is a strong first filter.

source: Piotrowski & Urban (2018) ATPboost: Learning Premise Selection in Binary Setting with ATP Feedback
finding: Train the premise selector with feedback from actual ATP runs (positive and negative), using gradient boosted trees in a loop.
numbers: Larger Mizar split (29,271 train, 3,253 test): 58.78% proved (1912) vs k-NN 50.81% (1653), a 15.7% relative gain. The paper notes the earlier deep-learning gain over k-NN was 4.3% (with much higher time limits).
limits: Feedback loop costs many ATP calls.
agent_relevance: Using the solver outcome as the training signal for retrieval (closed loop) beats imitating human reference proofs.

source: Bansal, Szegedy, Rabe, Loos, Toman (2020) Learning to Reason in Large Theories without Imitation (HOList)
finding: Prover for a large premise pool trained by RL without human proofs; exploration mixes in premises chosen by tf-idf lookup so it can discover useful premises.
numbers: Proved: pure imitation 49.95%; zero-human RL with explore 56.3% single checkpoint (64.2% cumulative); human-based RL 59.9% / 69.1%. Zero explore reaches over 90% of human-RL performance. Zero reference (no tf-idf exploration) only 7.0%.
limits: Exploration with tf-idf was essential: without it zero-human learning collapsed to 7.0%.
agent_relevance: A cheap lexical retriever as an exploration source lets an agent try facts it would never rank high. Keep a lexical fallback inside the loop.

source: Holden & Korovin (2023) Graph Sequence Learning for Premise Selection
finding: Image-captioning style: a pretrained GNN plus a language model generates the sequence of axioms needed.
numbers: 17.7% improvement gain over the baseline (SInE). iProver already solved 86% of problems in one subset without any selection, so gains there are limited.
limits: Large-theory TPTP-style tasks; baseline is a heuristic filter.
agent_relevance: Generating the premise list as a sequence is another set-aware route; gains shrink when the solver already copes with the pool.

source: Jiang, Li, Tworkowski, Wu, Szegedy et al. (2022) Thor: Wielding Hammers to Integrate Language Models and Automated Theorem Provers
finding: LM proposes proof steps and calls Sledgehammer (a hammer with its own premise selection) when a step needs premises. Splits the job: LM decides when, hammer decides which facts.
numbers: PISA: success 39.0% (LM alone) to 57.0% with Thor; Sledgehammer alone 25.7%; union 48.8%, so 8.2% of problems need both. LM-written steps naming premises advanced the proof only 1.9% of the time, vs 28.2% for steps with no premises. Variant where the LM learns to invoke the hammer by keywords: 55.4% (-1.6). MiniF2F 29.6% to 29.9%.
quote: 1.9% of the steps involving premise selection generated by the language model manage to advance the proof
limits: Hammer is a black box; gains depend on hammer quality.
agent_relevance: LMs are bad at naming library facts from memory (1.9% vs 28.2%). Hand that choice to a retriever or tool, and let the model decide when to call it.

source: Mikula, Tworkowski, Antoniak, Piotrowski, Jiang, Zhou, Szegedy, Kucinski, Milos, Wu (2024) Magnushammer
finding: Contrastive transformer retriever (select, then re-rank) for Isabelle. Beats Sledgehammer and lexical baselines on single-step and, combined with Thor, multi-step.
numbers: PISA single-step: BM25 30.6%, TF-IDF 31.8%, OpenAI embeddings 36.1%, Sledgehammer 38.3%, Magnushammer 59.5%. Multi-step: Thor 57.0% to Thor+Magnushammer 71.0% (4x fewer parameters than previous best). miniF2F test: Sledgehammer 10.4%, with heuristics 20.9%, Magnushammer 34.0%. Ensemble of all variants closes 65.5% in one step.
limits: Isabelle only; fine-tuned on own MAPL data (over 4M points); static scoring of one state.
agent_relevance: Off-the-shelf general embeddings (36.1%) were much worse than a retriever trained on the proof-state to premise task. Domain tuning is worth about 23 points.

source: Magnushammer (2024) data and size ablations
finding: Retriever is data-efficient and small models suffice. Pretraining matters most with little data.
numbers: 38M model, budget 800. With 0.1% of data (about 4K examples) and pretraining: 39.2% vs 16.8% without pretraining. Full data: 56.3% (MAPL) vs 54.0% (HPL), 53.0% without pretraining. A tiny 920K-parameter model reaches 40.7%, still above Sledgehammer 38.3%. Problems solved using at most k=8 premises: BM25 18.47%, MH-86M (MAPL, tactic prompt) 39.29%; at k=256: 30.55% vs 56.19%.
limits: Budget-800 numbers differ from the headline 59.5%.
agent_relevance: Even a tiny trained retriever beats a classical hammer. Quality at small k matters: a good ranker needs far fewer facts in the prompt.

source: Yang, Swope, Gu, Chalamala, Song, Yu, Godil, Prenger, Anandkumar (2023) LeanDojo: Theorem Proving with Retrieval-Augmented Language Models (ReProver)
finding: Dense retriever over accessible premises (mathlib) feeds a tactic generator (ReProver). Introduces in-file hard negatives and a novel_premises split.
numbers: Retrieval R@1/R@10/MRR, random split: BM25 6.7/17.2/0.15; ReProver 13.5/38.4/0.31. novel_premises: BM25 5.9/15.5/0.14; ReProver 9.1/27.6/0.24. Ablations (random): no in-file negatives 10.8/33.1; retrieving from all premises (not just accessible) 11.7/36.2. Pass@1 random: tidy 23.8, GPT-4 zero-shot 29.0, ReProver 51.2, ReProver without retrieval 47.6. novel_premises: 5.3 / 7.4 / 26.3 / 23.2. MiniF2F 26.5%, ProofNet 13.8%.
limits: Retrieval adds 3.6 points on the random split and 3.1 on novel_premises, much smaller than the retriever's gain over BM25 suggests. GPT-4 data contamination possible.
agent_relevance: Restrict candidates to what is accessible (scope filtering) and mine hard negatives from the same file or context. Retrieval gain is real but modest when the generator is already strong.

source: LeanDojo (2023) generalisation to unseen premises
finding: Performance drops sharply when test proofs need premises never seen in training, showing retrievers partly memorise.
numbers: novel_premises vs random: retriever R@10 27.6 vs 38.4; Pass@1 26.3 vs 51.2 for ReProver (about halved). GPT-4 7.4 vs 29.0.
limits: Authors argue novel_premises is the more honest benchmark.
agent_relevance: Test our subgoal library retrieval on goals whose best entry is new or rarely used, not on entries seen during tuning.

source: Piotrowski, Fernandez Mir, Ayers (2023) Machine-Learned Premise Selection for Lean
finding: Lightweight random forest in Lean 4 (suggest_premises tactic) versus k-NN. Trained online; names plus bigrams as features.
numbers: Cover metric: all-premises filter RF n+b 0.57 vs k-NN 0.52; source filter 0.29 vs 0.25; math filter 0.26 vs 0.23. Trigrams hurt (0.16 on math filter, overfit). Speed: RF 0.28 s vs k-NN 5.65 s per theorem. On the harder intermediate set: RF Cover 0.09 / Cover+ 0.24; k-NN 0.08 / 0.21.
limits: Scores inflated on the all filter by trivial rfl-type lemmas. Real tasks reach only 0.09 cover.
agent_relevance: Easy items inflate retrieval metrics. Report separately on hard goals, and keep the selector fast enough to call at every step.

source: Zhu, Clune, Avigad, Jiang, Welleck (2026) Premise Selection for a Lean Hammer (LeanPremise / LeanHammer)
finding: First end-to-end Lean hammer: neural premise selector, translation to external provers, proof reconstruction. Selector adapts to user-local lemmas.
numbers: Mathlib-test: with the large (82M) selector, 33.3% proved (cumul), 37.3% accumulated over sizes; ground-truth premises give 43.0% (ceiling). Recall@32 67.8% to 72.7% with size, full proof rate 27.9% to 30.1%. Against MePo: recall@32 73% higher relative, proof rate 21% higher. Union neural + MePo gives 34.5%. miniCTX-v2: share of ground-truth-solvable theorems that get solved 79.4% vs 73.5% on Mathlib. With no premises results are much worse. Retrained ReProver is clearly lower.
limits: Failures: missed premises, Lean-auto translation, limits of Aesop and Zipperposition.
agent_relevance: Neural and symbolic selectors solve different goals, so run both. The pipeline is near its ceiling given ground-truth premises, so the next gain is in the solver stage, not retrieval.

source: Petrovcic, Narvaez, Todorovski (2025) Combining Textual and Structural Information for Premise Selection in Lean
finding: Add a GNN over a dependency graph (state-premise and premise-premise edges) to dense text embeddings.
numbers: LeanDojo test: ReProver R@1 13.42%, R@10 39.60%, MRR 0.3283; GNN-augmented 17.98% (+33.98%), 50.04% (+26.36%), 0.4095 (+24.73%); with EMA 18.31%, 50.33%, 0.4140. Ablation: dropping context graph gives R@10 49.99 vs 48.52 no-ablation run; dropping premise graph 49.30. So ablations move little.
limits: Ablation differences are small and sometimes inverted; retrieval only, no proof success reported.
agent_relevance: Relations between library entries (what depends on or co-occurs with what) help rank them. Store links between subgoal entries.

source: Tao, Liu, Wang, Xu (2025) Learning an Effective Premise Retrieval Model for Efficient Mathematical Formalization
finding: Lightweight contrastive retriever with formal-language tokenizer, fine-grained similarity and re-ranker; compared with ReProver and general embedders.
numbers: Random split R@1/R@5/R@10: ReProver 11.79/28.78/36.69; ours 15.17/38.20/46.53; general embedders (UniXcoder, E5-large-v2, BGE-m3) 4.0-4.4 / 18.6-19.5 / 25.3-27.3. Novel-premise split (RI) R@10: ReProver 19.48, ours 30.91, embedders 23.8-24.7 (embedders beat ReProver there).
limits: Workshop paper; retrieval metrics only.
agent_relevance: General text embedders are weak at this task, yet generalise better than an over-fitted retriever to unseen premises.

source: Ju & Dong (2025) MIRB: Mathematical Information Retrieval Benchmark
finding: Benchmark with 12 datasets across question-answer, premise and formula retrieval, including NaturalProofs, LeanDojo (2,060 queries, 180,944 documents) and MAPL (4,109 queries, 493,029 documents).
numbers: Dataset statistics only: LeanDojo uses the novel_premises split; MAPL is Isabelle; NaturalProofs is natural-language premise retrieval.
limits: I read the dataset section; I did not extract per-model scores.
agent_relevance: A ready test bed to check an embedding model for our retrieval step before building our own.

source: Gao, Sun, Jiang, Wang et al. (2026) LeanSearch v2: Global Premise Retrieval for Lean 4 Theorem Proving
finding: Defines global premise retrieval: recover the whole premise set a theorem needs, not one step's lemmas. Reasoning-mode retriever with LLM query planning and a judge loop.
numbers: MathlibMPR (69 queries): reasoning mode recovers 46.1% of ground-truth premise groups within 10 candidates; strongest reasoning retrievers 38.0% (DIVER); premise-selection baselines 9.3%. Sketch accepted by the judge for 46 of 69 queries (66.7%); 29 (42.0%) accepted at first draft; 23 (33.3%) failed after 3 revisions. MathlibQR Recall@10 for standard mode: easy 0.829, hard 0.722.
limits: Authors built both benchmark and system. Prover is Claude Sonnet 4.5 with 8 reflection rounds.
agent_relevance: Single-step selectors score 9.3% on whole-proof premise sets. For an agent that plans first, retrieve for the whole plan with an LLM-written query, then verify.

source: LeanSearch v2 (2026) downstream proof test, Table 3
finding: Same prover loop, only the retriever changed. Better retrieval gave more proofs.
numbers: FATE-H (n=100) solved: no retrieval 4 (4.0%); LeanFinder 12 (12.0%); INF-X-Retriever 7 (7.0%); LeanSearch v2 standard 16 (16.0%); reasoning mode 20 (20.0%), best. MathlibMPR-Prop (n=50): no retrieval 2 (4%); LeanFinder 5 (10%); standard 5 (10%); reasoning 7 (14%).
limits: Small n (50 and 100), so one problem is 1-2 points; no confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: Retrieval turned 4% into 16-20% in an agent-style reflection loop. Retrieval is a main lever for loop-based provers, even with a strong LLM.

source: Lu, Emond, Yang, Chaudhuri, Sun, Chen (2026) Lean Finder: Semantic Search for Mathlib That Understands User Intents
finding: Search engine tuned on synthesized user queries and preference feedback. Compared with other search tools and GPT-4o.
numbers: Real-user preference (LMArena style): Lean Finder 81.6% vs Lean Search 56.9% vs GPT-4o 54.1%. Claims 30%+ relative gain on retrieval metrics. Plugged into whole-proof provers (w/o vs w/ LF): Goedel-Prover-SFT miniF2F pass@1 38.1% to 38.5%, ProofNet 6.6% to 7.2%; DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5-RL ProofNet pass@1 4.3% to 6.5%, pass@32 14.5% to 18.3%; PutnamBench inconsistent (e.g. 7 vs 6 at budget 32).
limits: Downstream gains are small (0 to 3.8 points) and absent on hard PutnamBench; authors say provers cannot yet use retrieved statements for hard problems.
agent_relevance: Better retrieval does not help if the model cannot use what it gets. Check the consumer, not only the retriever.

source: Kozyrev, Khramov, Solovev, Podkopaev (2026) RocqStar: Similarity-driven Retrieval and Agentic Systems for Rocq generation
finding: Self-attentive embedder trained so statements with similar proofs are close (proof-aware, not statement-aware). Used inside a multi-stage agent with planning, debate and reflection.
numbers: Up to 28% relative gain in generator performance over statement-similarity retrieval. Agent proves 60% of the CoqPilot dataset vs 51% for the best earlier result (Claude 3.5 Sonnet). Debate in planning: +20% relative overall. Ablation on its split: Full Agent 66% overall; without planning 56%; without reflection 58%. Reflection forces retrieval and re-planning after failed attempts.
limits: Gain from the retriever is moderate in the agentic setting: the agent hides some weak retrieval.
agent_relevance: Index entries by what their solutions look like, not by what their statements look like. Retry-triggered re-retrieval after failure is a working loop pattern.

source: Zhang, Borchert, Gritta, Lampouras (2026) DRIFT: Decompose, Retrieve, Illustrate, then Formalize Theorems
finding: LLM splits a statement into sub-queries before retrieving premises, then adds example theorems that show usage.
numbers: Dependency-retrieval F1 up by 13.34 (ProofNet), 2.08 (miniF2F-test), 7.74 (ConNF) points on average over no decomposition. ConNF BEq+@10 +42.25% (GPT-4.1) and +37.14% (DeepSeek-V3.1). Ablation GPT-4.1 ConNF BEq+@1: full 54.84; w/o Illustrate 35.90; w/o Decompose 46.72; w/o retrieval 4.47. miniF2F has 0.43 library dependencies on average: extra context acts as a distractor. Decomposer LLMs differ by at most 2.05 F1.
limits: Gain depends on whether the model already knows the library. Parametric retrieval (model recalls names) lost 40-55 points on ConNF.
agent_relevance: Query decomposition helps; usage examples guard against misuse. When few facts are needed, extra retrieved context hurts, so let the agent skip retrieval.

source: Yang et al. (2025) FormalML: Benchmark for Formal Subgoal Completion in Machine Learning Theory
finding: 4,937 subgoal-completion problems; 2,049 require explicit premise retrieval (Mathlib or local). Tests provers given M candidate premises (true ones mixed with random) at M=10 and M=20.
numbers: Most models improve with candidates, but performance declines as M grows from 10 to 20. DeepSeek-Prover-V2 gains about 10% at M=10; STP, strong overall, underperforms with premises (no such training data).
limits: Candidates are random distractors, not retrieval-model outputs; exact table figures not extracted.
agent_relevance: Models differ widely in ability to pick useful facts from a list. More distractors cost accuracy, so keep the shown list short.

source: Ji (2026) CSLibPremiseBench: Structure-Guided Premise Retrieval and Label Robustness for Lean 4 CS Theorems
finding: Careful near-null study: a structure-aware graph-lexical reranker barely beats lexical BM25 on a CS library, and proxy labels are weak.
numbers: 801 tasks, 1,875 candidate declarations. CSG-Rerank MRR 0.5236 vs BM25 0.5061 (+0.0175, 95% CI [+0.0016,+0.0335]) but not better than BM25+symbol (+0.0037, CI [-0.0103,+0.0173]); no gain in Recall@10. Label audit: 2666 of 2845 proxy links kept (93.7%); only 462 of 958 (48.2%) appear in elaborated terms.
limits: Single author; labels are text-reference proxies, not real dependencies; no proof-generation test.
agent_relevance: Simple lexical plus symbol overlap is hard to beat. Beware labels that only approximate what was truly used.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) LeanHammer paper, comparison with ReProver and MePo
finding: Authors re-trained ReProver with its own scripts on their splits and an updated Mathlib, and re-ran the Piotrowski random-forest selector as an upper bound.
numbers: LeanPremise beats both in recall and proof rate. The text notes recall@k numbers differ from Yang et al. 2023 because the upper-bound definition differs (they checked manually).
limits: Numbers across papers are not comparable without matching splits and metric definitions.
agent_relevance: Treat cross-paper retrieval numbers with care; re-run baselines on our own library.

source: Li et al. (2024) A Survey on Deep Learning for Theorem Proving
finding: Survey section 3.2 traces premise selection from binary classification (Irving 2016) to GNNs, contrastive transformers and dense retrieval, and notes joint training of tactic prediction with premise selection (ReProver).
numbers: Retrieval metrics R@k and MRR are standard; Magnushammer and ReProver are cited as the main gains on unseen premises.
limits: Secondary source; counted only for the field map.
agent_relevance: Gives the lineage: classifier, then graph, then dense retriever, then retrieval inside the agent loop.

source: Natural Language Premise Selection: Finding Supporting Statements for Mathematical Text (2020)
finding: Seen in arXiv search only: premise selection from natural-language mathematical text. Not opened.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Candidate follow-up on informal-to-informal premise retrieval.
